hints: Start from the F1 parents - both are AaBb on different chromosomes, so think about how many different combinations of A/a with B/b can go into one gamete.
Recall the rule given in the stem - any genotype with at least one A is white, only aa allows B or b to be seen.
Fill the 4x4 grid systematically by combining one gamete from each parent, then decide colour for each box by checking the A locus first.
Count how many boxes are white versus yellow (aaB-) versus green (aabb) to write the final ratio in simplest whole numbers.
walkthrough:
Work Out The F1 Gametes**
Both F1 parents are AaBb and the two genes are on different chromosomes. Each gamete gets one allele of each gene, so four types are possible in equal proportions: $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$ and $ab$. Put these across the top and down the side of Fig. 2.1.

Apply The Epistasis Rule**
Allele A is dominant epistatic. That means if the genotype contains $A-$, the fruit is white no matter what B/b is present. Only when the genotype is $aa$ can you see the second gene: $aaB-$ is yellow and $aabb$ is green. This is not normal 9:3:3:1.

Fill And Count The Square**
Combine gametes to give the 16 genotypes, e.g. $AB \times AB = AABB$ white, $aB \times ab = aaBb$ yellow, $ab \times ab = aabb$ green. Counting boxes: 9 $A-B-$ + 3 $A-bb$ = 12 white, 3 $aaB-$ = 3 yellow, 1 $aabb$ = 1 green.

State The Ratio**
Ratio of fruit colours in F2 = 12 white : 3 yellow : 1 green.
Final answer: Gametes: AB, Ab, aB, ab from each parent. F2 genotypes as in 4x4 Punnett square. Phenotypes: A- B- and A- bb all white, aaB- yellow, aabb green. Ratio: 12 white : 3 yellow : 1 green.

hints: The green-fruited pollen parent can only be aabb, so it can only give ab gametes - the offspring phenotypes must therefore reveal what P and Q gave.
Both P and Q are white so must contain A, but look at whether they produced yellow (aaB-) or green (aabb) offspring to work out if they could give aB or ab gametes.
walkthrough:
Fix The Tester Genotype**
Green fruit is only $aabb$, so the pollen parent gives only $ab$ gametes. Any $A$ or $B$ in the offspring must have come from P or Q.

Deduce P And Q**
For P: 1/2 white ($AaB-$) : 1/2 yellow ($aaB-$). To get $aa$ in half the offspring, P must be $Aa$, and to give only $B$ gametes (no green $aabb$ appears), P must be $BB$. So P = $AaBB$. For Q: 1/2 white ($AaBb$) : 1/2 green ($aabb$). To get $aa$ and $bb$ in half, Q must be $Aa$ and $bb$. So Q = $Aabb$.
Final answer: plant P: AaBB; plant Q: Aabb.

hints: The two genes are on different chromosomes, so think about what happens to whole maternal and paternal chromosomes when they line up.
Focus on the stage where homologous pairs line up at the equator and their orientation is random - which division and which phase is this?
walkthrough:
Name The Source Of New Combinations**
Because A/a and B/b are on different chromosomes, the maternal and paternal homologues can line up either way round. This random orientation produces new combinations of alleles in gametes, called independent or random assortment.

Pinpoint When It Happens**
This lining up of homologous chromosome pairs at the equator occurs at metaphase I of meiosis. Separation at anaphase I then locks in the different $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$ gametes.
Final answer: process: independent / random assortment of chromosomes; stage of meiosis: metaphase I.

hints: Compare the two breeding methods - one mixes existing squash alleles, the other brings in DNA from outside squash.
Think of the technical term for an organism that contains foreign DNA from a different species made in the laboratory.
walkthrough:
Spot The Foreign DNA**
Tigress was made by selective breeding, which only reshuffles squash alleles already present. Freedom II had genes for viral coat proteins added to the squash genome, so its cells contain DNA from two different organisms - squash plus virus.

Link To Recombinant**
Combining DNA from different sources in this way is recombinant DNA technology. Freedom II is therefore the recombinant, transgenic or genetically modified organism.
Final answer: Freedom II; contains viral / foreign DNA / genes from two different sources / organisms, so produced by genetic engineering / genetic modification / transgenic GMO.

hints: If plants resist virus, think about what happens to food supply and farmer income compared with a crop that dies.
For the downside, think about consumer worries about eating new viral proteins or about acceptance of GM crops in society.
walkthrough:
State A Social Advantage**
Resistant plants survive viral disease, so yield is maintained and more food is available. Farmers do not lose their crop and income, which benefits the community.

State A Social Disadvantage**
The added viral coat protein is a new protein in food and might trigger allergy in some people. There may also be public mistrust or ethical objection to growing and eating GM squash.
Final answer: advantage: improved yield / crop not lost as plants do not die of disease; disadvantage: viral proteins might cause allergies / social / ethical resistance to GM crops.
